Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (PHCUs/PHCCs) in South Sudan record patient data using paper registers and handwritten monthly summary reports, which are physically delivered to County Health Departments (CHDs). CHDs then transcribe these into DHIS2 for aggregate reporting. No evidence of electronic health records or digital entry at point-of-care in rural clinics; facilities lack infrastructure (electricity, internet, hardware). A 2020 pilot provided tablets for DHIS2 entry in 57 HIV facilities, but expansion stalled due to overburdened staff and infrastructure gaps. SMS used for weekly disease surveillance aggregates (not patient records) in some pilots, replacing paper delivery but sourced from paper forms. Recent 2023 study in Maridi County rural PHCCs confirms all use manual methods. Key barriers: conflict, poor roads, staff shortages, no connectivity, low capacity. National DHIS2 ambition exists at CHD/state levels, but rural point-of-service remains entirely paper-based (score 1), with digital limited to aggregation.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is supported by the cited World Bank Routine Health Information Systems brief, which confirms rural PHCU/PHCC staff transcribe paper registers into monthly reports hand-delivered to County Health Departments for DHIS2 entry, as facilities lack the infrastructure for facility-level entry. Cross-checked against the WHO South Sudan Health Information System Maturity Assessment (February 2025), which records comprehensive facility-wide electronic systems at only 22.4% of health facilities nationally (concentrated in larger, urban-adjacent facilities), and a DHIS2 Community note on the Boma Health Initiative digitalisation pilot (March 2025-February 2026), which remains an early-stage community-health-worker pilot rather than a clinic point-of-care system. No evidence found of routine digital data capture in rural clinics. Score confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (PHCUs/PHCCs) in South Sudan record patient data on paper registers and handwritten monthly summary reports, which are physically carried to County Health Departments for transcription into the national DHIS2 platform. Facility-level electronic systems remain rare, covering an estimated 22% of health facilities nationally and concentrated away from rural primary care. A Boma Health Initiative DHIS2 Tracker pilot running from 2025 to 2026 is testing digital data capture by community health workers on Android devices, but this remains an early-stage pilot confined to selected counties. Persistent constraints of electricity, connectivity, staffing and infrastructure keep point-of-care data capture in rural clinics entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in South Sudan record criminal cases and complaints using entirely manual, paper-based systems such as handwritten dockets and pen-and-paper documentation, as evidenced by studies on stations like Malakia central police station (not rural but indicative) describing the system as "purely manual" and proposals for digitization planned initially for cities/towns. No evidence found of digital case management systems, computers, or IT infrastructure deployed at rural point-of-service facilities; searches across general web, academic papers, World Bank, UN/UNDP/USAID reports yielded only urban initiatives (e.g., Juba surveillance cameras, judiciary portals, personnel digitization from 2012). Key barriers include chronic conflict, limited resources, lack of electricity/infrastructure, illiteracy among officers, and weak national capacity, as noted in OSAC and Small Arms Survey reports on SSNPS challenges outside capitals. National policy focuses on reform and community policing but shows vast gap with rural reality, where customary justice dominates due to ineffective statutory policing; no pilots or donor projects indicate routine digital use at rural stations.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is broadly supported by the cited case study of Malakia central police station, which describes a "purely manual" pen-and-paper criminal records system, and by Small Arms Survey and US State Department reporting on severe logistics and infrastructure gaps facing police in rural areas (lack of vehicles, radios, weapons; police stations sometimes unstaffed for weeks). A further search for 2023-2026 evidence found only personnel-registration digitisation (SSNPS ID cards, dating to 2011-2013, HR/payroll only) and a 2026 laptop donation to the judiciary (a separate institution, not police case records) - no evidence emerged of case or incident record digitisation reaching rural police stations. The underlying evidence is indicative (an urban case study and national-level infrastructure reporting) rather than rural-specific, so this is confirmed on a thinner evidence base than the other rows in this batch, though consistent across all sources found. Score confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in South Sudan record criminal cases and complaints using entirely manual, paper-based systems, including handwritten dockets and case files. A case study of police record-keeping practice (Malakia central police station) describes the criminal records process as "purely manual", reliant on pen-and-paper documentation, with digitisation proposals aimed initially at cities and towns rather than rural stations. Constraints of poor infrastructure, absent electricity and connectivity, limited logistics (vehicles, radios) and low capacity are especially acute in rural and remote areas, where community policing arrangements and customary justice mechanisms often substitute for statutory policing. Personnel identity registration has been digitised in parts of the force for human-resource purposes, but this does not extend to case or incident records at rural stations.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in South Sudan rely entirely on paper-based recording for births and other vital events, using manual forms and registers like traditional birth certificates with handwritten serial numbers, dates, and names. No evidence found of digital systems at point-of-service in rural facilities; birth registration coverage remains very low (~1-10% estimated from anecdotes), with services inaccessible due to conflict, poor infrastructure, and understaffing. Recent developments include the 2018 Civil Registry Act and 2024 Regulations establishing legal framework, plus pilots for birth registration in Juba (urban) supported by Vital Strategies/UNHCR, but these are isolated and not scaled to rural areas. A costed CRVS plan exists, but implementation lags due to institutional weaknesses, electricity shortages (only ~5% national access), no internet in rural areas, ongoing violence, and funding gaps. National ambitions for CRVS strengthening contrast sharply with rural reality, where paper processes prevail and even notification is minimal; digitization scores <35% per 2017 UNECA assessment, with 0% death registration per 2025 WHO report. Score 1 conservative given lack of rural-specific digital evidence.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed and strengthened by an October 2024 statement from South Sudan's Minister of Interior (reported by Eye Radio) that the civil registry system remains unintegrated and is effectively limited to towns, with the majority of citizens in rural settings unreached by it. This corroborates the cited APAI-CRVS/UNECA and WHO assessments describing low digitisation and coverage nationally. No evidence found of digital data capture at rural registry points. revised_comments: Rural civil registry services in South Sudan remain entirely paper-based, using manual forms and handwritten registers for birth and other vital event notifications. Birth registration coverage is low, and the Minister of Interior has stated publicly that the civil registry system operates mainly in towns and is not integrated, with the majority of citizens in rural settings unreached by it. The 2018 Civil Registration Act and 2024 regulations establish a legal framework, and pilot digitisation efforts (such as birth notification integrated into community health outreach) exist in limited counties, but these have not scaled to routine digital data capture at rural registry points. Electricity access, connectivity and institutional capacity constraints in rural areas keep the point-of-service process entirely manual.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in South Sudan predominantly use handwritten classroom registers and paper record books for attendance, enrollment, and administrative data, which are aggregated manually at state level for national EMIS reporting. Recent 2026 AU IPED assessment traces data flow from paper at school level, with field visits confirming reliance on paper tools even in Juba schools; rural areas face worse ICT deficits (no computers, internet, power). The 2023 National Education Census involved enumerators visiting schools for headcounts and data capture, indicating no routine digital POS systems. Pilots like SSSAMS (SMS-based attendance via phones, donor-funded GESS project 2013-2020, still partially used) represent isolated digital elements, but not standard at most rural facilities. National EMIS exists for aggregation, but rural point-of-service remains paper-based. Key barriers: conflict, inadequate infrastructure/connectivity esp rural, low capacity, donor dependency. Gap: Policy aims for EMIS strengthening/digital census tools, but rural reality is manual due to logistics/power shortages.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed by a fresh April 2026 GPE KIX/AU IPED report on South Sudan's Education Management Information System, which states that education data collection "still begins with handwritten registers" and that there is "continued reliance on manual data collection at the school level", particularly outside urban areas. The donor-funded SSSAMS SMS attendance system and its ODK-based direct-digital option provide isolated digital capture in a small number of participating schools (the system's own live dashboard shows only around two dozen schools actively reporting attendance out of thousands nationally), which is consistent with the original assessment that these are not representative of rural point-of-service practice generally. Score confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in South Sudan capture attendance, enrolment and administrative data through handwritten classroom registers, which are aggregated manually for state and national Education Management Information System reporting. A 2026 African Union assessment of the system confirms that education data collection still begins with handwritten registers and that manual data collection persists at school level, particularly outside urban areas where infrastructure and connectivity are weakest. A donor-funded SMS-based attendance system (SSSAMS, part of the Girls' Education South Sudan programme) and an ODK-based direct-digital data entry option exist, but active participation is limited to a small number of schools nationally, and rural point-of-service data capture remains predominantly paper-based.
